On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open-source everything.
That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI , as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.
Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. It specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI and other heavyweights and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify and Notion. Co-founder Chenyu Zhao and I spoke on stage toward the end of the day.
Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July .
Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets.
Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks . Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them.
Fireworks, assigned a $17.5 billion valuation by its investors in summer, is reportedly in “ early talks ” for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment.
There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute , which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock.
Here’s some of what Zhao had to say. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
You spent a decade at Google , including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did?
When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with.
How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it?
I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator.
A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three.
If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch?
Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 users and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source.
In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice , once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect?
We think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token.
Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction.
On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public.
Fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers?
Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised.
Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers?
I don’t think I can publicly name the specific customers that were impacted. Some, such as Notion and Cursor, have gone public already. It was a small subset of our customers that had this data impact.
How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise?
Notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. We’re moving those services to an online flow so we keep data only as long as we need it.
Jensen Huang left Nvidia last week, and Nvidia has backed Fireworks since 2024. Does that affect you ?
It’s been a blow to the industry, and we feel for Jensen and his family. But Nvidia has always been a strong supporter of open source, and I don’t see that changing. We expect it to keep investing in Nemotron, and we’re excited to keep partnering with them.

Australian physicists chose to transmit the word ‘gravity’ in binary code through brick wall
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom.
Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement.
The research, published in the journal Science Advances , involved a sensitive detection device known as a gravimeter, which was set up on the floor of a men’s bathroom adjacent to the lift.
The gravimeter was able to detect the position of the elevator’s 1.8-tonne counterweight as it moved between two levels – representing 0 and 1 in binary code – which enabled the scientists to send a message.
The experiment is reminiscent of a plot point in the Christopher Nolan film Interstellar , in which a gravitational anomaly creates messages in binary code.
The researchers chose to transmit the word “gravity”, or 1000111 1110010 1100001 1110110 1101001 1110100 1111001 in binary code. At a transmission rate of one bit (digit) per minute, the single word took nearly an hour to send.
The scientists say that while gravitational communication is currently far from usable given its extremely slow speed, an advantage is that it is a “practically unblockable wireless communication scheme”.
“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” said co-author Dr Charles Woffinden, of UQ’s school of mathematics and physics. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with wifi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”
Study co-author Prof Matthew Davis told Guardian Australia: “At the moment, it’s very hard to imagine how it could be practically useful.” But he added that the experiment was “theoretically interesting enough that it was worth doing”.
To put into perspective how slow the message transmission was, Davis said that Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which after 49 years of travel had just reached a distance of one light-day away, could “communicate with Earth at a faster data rate than our communication concept”.
According to Davis, the new method of communicating could theoretically occur at ranges of up to 500 metres and at a rate 15 times faster, if more sensitive quantum gravity sensors were used.
The idea for the elevator study arose from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge – which would use quantum sensors to detect changes in the strength of gravity due to a passing truck, allowing scientists to determine the mass of a large vehicle.
Classical gravimeters can be thought of as a mass on a spring. “If you stretch the spring, the mass bounces up and down at a certain rate, which is determined by the spring and the gravitational field,” Davis said. “If the gravitational field changes ever so slightly, the rate at which it bounces back and forth changes.
“Sometimes doing physics leads in unexpected ways and it’s a bit of fun … you get to do quirky things on the side. It’s one of the great joys of science to have stuff like this happen.”
Other near-unblockable methods of communication – involving neutrinos or gravitational waves – have been proposed “but these approaches are somewhat hindered by the difficulty in generating a measurable signal”, the scientists note.
The physicists conducted the research in UQ’s Parnell physics building, which is also home to the world’s longest-running science experiment – the pitch drop experiment , which began in 1927.

CEO Elon Musk said SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching.
These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk said, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week.
“We’ve got a plan that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk said, noting the company is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold. “But there is a missing piece of the puzzle here which is that if you’re indoors, especially if you have a metal roof, that blocks the signal from space. So we need something that’s terrestrial that addresses situations where people are, you know, in a building with a thick roof essentially.”
The company’s efforts initially focused on buying wireless spectrum after receiving the Federal Communications Commission’s approval in 2024 to move forward with plans to offer a direct-to-phone version of its Starlink satellite internet service, in partnership with T-Mobile. SpaceX struck a $17 billion deal with EchoStar in 2025 and agreed this year to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum valued at $8 billion.
Combining that wireless spectrum with mini cell towers should boost signals and end the dead zone problem, he said. According to Musk, the company has completed the design of what he described as “a micro cell tower thing that you just put on your roof, like a Starlink dish.”
Musk, who has a history of missing his own production deadlines, demurred, saying the devices were “going into production, I think, next year.”
The idea isn’t new, but it wasn’t clear until this week how much progress SpaceX had made toward developing the hardware.
SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said during the company’s August earnings call that it wouldn’t use big cell towers and would instead deploy small, low-power cellular base stations.
Even with this latest progress report, SpaceX appears to be still working out the details. Musk said one approach would be to bundle the small cellular base stations together with Starlink terminals.
SpaceX’s plan to build a hybrid cellular-satellite network has fueled speculation, and even predictions, that legacy telecom companies could be in danger. But Musk doesn’t think so, because he expects an entirely new class of customers to drive demand for wireless bandwidth: AI.
“I don’t think this means, like you know, AT&T, Verizon, or others go out of business or anything,” he said, adding that maybe they’ll lose some revenue. “But I actually think that the demand for bandwidth will be tremendous in the future, and a lot, and that bandwidth will be driven primarily by superintelligence and robots, and they’re going to need a lot more bandwidth than humans.”

There’s a new way to keep an eye on your AI usage and when your limits reset: by using your Mac’s app icons. Yes, really!
Designer Michael Flarup has just launched a new Mac utility called IconSwapper , which lets you replace any app’s official icon with one of your own creation. While you can use this tool to change your icons’ appearance, design, shading, and more, one of the more interesting ways to use it is to swap the icons for AI apps like ChatGPT or Claude with versions that can display your live AI usage.
Doing so is fairly simple, and you don’t have to be technically minded to get this to work. After installing the app on your Mac, you simply choose which application you want to create a “live” icon for — meaning one that responds to a particular app.
Besides tracking AI usage in ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, you can also create live icons for a number of the built-in Mac apps like Messages, Mail, Safari, Finder, Music, and others like Chrome and Spotify, but these configurations tend to be more fun than they are practical. For instance, you can configure Safari’s compass to follow things like page loads and downloads, or you can make it so that the Finder guy’s eyes follow your cursor around the screen. (That one is hilarious!)
Of course, there are plenty of other ways to track your AI usage — you don’t need an icon to do that. You can track usage from your account or your harness, even from a fun little gadget . But tracking it from the icon adds a certain whimsy to your Mac desktop setup. (If your dock is crowded, note that you can also see your icon customizations from your tab bar as you switch apps.)
Beyond live icons, you can also change what an icon looks like using IconSwapper’s built-in tools.
There are a surprising number of built-in customizations that are as easy to use as clicking a few buttons or toggling a switch. IconSwapper also comes with a large library of alternative icons for every app that are already ready to use, or you can upload your own.
Flarup is based in Copenhagen, where he runs a design studio , and he has been drawn to icon design and customization for years. He’s been making his own Mac icons since the early 2000s and even wrote a book about app icons that celebrates the work of designers.
He had been working on a solution that would allow him to customize Mac icons, which had proven tricky because macOS has no official support for theming and protects its system icons. To work around this, he came up with a different technique that involves drawing directly on the icons without replacing them, allowing him to use shaders, motion, and display real data.
Flarup tells TechCrunch that his renderer runs the icon artwork through custom Metal shaders in real time.
“The breakthrough was figuring out how to send the Dock a bitmap for another running app and have it draw that frame itself,” he explained. “I spent a lot of time getting the artwork to follow the icon through all the little ways macOS moves it, from Dock magnification to the Command-Tab switcher. Once I had that working, I could make the icon react to whatever’s happening,” Flarup said.
That lets users configure icons to do all kinds of fun, new things they never could before, like make light move across a gold icon as you drag your cursor over it, or animate an app’s icon while it’s thinking.
“That opens up a lot of fun ways to make your Mac feel like yours. I’ve always felt the software we use every day could be a little more fun and a lot more personal,” he added.
The app itself is a one-time purchase of $19 as a launch promo but will later sell for $29, its website says.

The International Court of Justice has found Myanmar guilty of genocide against its Rohingya minority. It is the first time in the court’s 80-year history that it has ruled a state committed the crime.
"The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said on Thursday, reading the verdict in The Hague, Netherlands.
For almost three hours, Iwasawa set out the evidence from the military’s 2017 campaign against the mostly Muslim Rohingya, which drove hundreds of thousands of people across the border into Bangladesh.
He said Myanmar's security forces had killed thousands of Rohingya civilians and committed "widespread sexual violence" against women and "extreme violence" against children.
The judges found that Rohingya villages had been systematically destroyed and resettled with non-Rohingya people. They concluded that the "only reasonable inference" was that Myanmar intended to destroy the group, which is the legal test for genocide.
The court ordered Myanmar to compensate the Rohingya for "the damage caused by the violations of its obligations... in so far as such damage is not made good by restitution". The amount will be decided at a later date.
Myanmar must also "allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return" of those who fled, and investigate and punish anyone suspected of taking part in the genocide.
ICJ rulings are binding and cannot be appealed. However, the court has no power to enforce them, and it is unclear whether Myanmar’s leaders will comply.
The verdict is likely to add to pressure on Min Aung Hlaing, who led the military during the 2017 crackdown. He seized power from Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in a 2021 coup, and this year he was installed as civilian president after tightly restricted elections. The ruling could complicate his push for international recognition.
Agnes Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International, called the ruling "a historic and authoritative recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya and a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families".
Legal experts are watching the case for signs of how the ICJ might rule on South Africa's separate case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
More than a million Rohingya now live in the world’s largest refugee camp, across the border in Bangladesh. Refugees there have described gang rapes, mass executions and attacks on families and children.
"I want justice," said a 23-year-old survivor of rape, speaking to AFP before the verdict from the cramped shelter she shares with her family. She asked not to be named.
"There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women," she said.
Mohammed Osman, 20, said he hoped the ruling would let him go home to perform last rites for his parents and younger brother, who were killed by the military.
"They shot my father dead, forced my mother into a house with a few other women, raped them and burnt down our homestead," he told AFP.
The Gambia brought the case in 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention, which allows any signatory state to take another to court over suspected breaches. It has the backing of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
"It is not about esoteric issues of international law, it is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings," said Dawda Jallow, The Gambia’s justice minister.
Myanmar has always denied genocide. It says it was responding to an insurgency after militant attacks killed about a dozen members of its security forces.
"Myanmar was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free rein," Ko Ko Hlaing, Myanmar’s representative, told the judges at hearings in January.

Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes
Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.
The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.
The ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said a majority of nine judges on the 15-seat court found that “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya”.
The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.
Nearly a decade later, in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, crowds of Rohingya people watching on outdoor TV screens leaped up in celebration and applause as the final verdict was read out.
One Rohingya survivor, Yousuf Ali, had travelled to the court to hear the verdict. “Today, we have finally been heard, and it is a profound relief,” he said. “This judgment gives hope to our children and the next generation of Rohingya. But our fight is not over.”
Governments had been anxiously awaiting the decision handed down in the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel .
In what could become a crucial factor for the Gaza case, where Israel claims its mass killings are part of a counter-terrorism operation, judges dismissed Myanmar’s claims of carrying out legitimate military operations against insurgents.
Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention , is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Iwasawa said during the reading of the decision that the court was “fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar”.
After the ruling, Britain’s foreign minister, Ed Miliband, said the government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attaché and called “urgently” for a session at the UN security council, the body that has the power to enforce ICJ rulings.
The case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.
In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who had travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than a million Rohingya still live there, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.
Refugees who had fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli , where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down , was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.
During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”. “It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.
The court appeared to back that assessment, accusing the military of using sexual violence to “physically and mentally impair the willingness and ability of the [Rohingya] population to procreate”, referring to cultural stigma for rape survivors. Myanmar had also imposed other measures to restrict births, the court ruled, such as limits of two children per Rohingya family.
Myanmar has denied carrying out a genocide, claiming its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.
However, judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states, on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
During a reading of the decision that lasted more than two hours in a packed Great Hall of Justice in The Hague, Iwasawa called for Myanmar to provide reparations and restitution. This included allowing the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, returning or replacing their property, and providing physical and mental rehabilitation.
The ruling was also significant as it formally classified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group under international law, something they have been denied by Myanmar, which refers to them as Bengalis or foreign migrants.
Reached by phone shortly after he left the courtroom, the ​lead counsel for the case against Myanmar told the Guardian the mood had been emotional in the room as the judgment was read out in front of his legal team, which included Rohingya.
“This is the ICJ recognising their history of discrimination, recognising them as a group, recognising the horrific violence they endured and suffered,” said Arsalan Suleman. “It was a really emotional moment for them and the whole team. We felt the weight of the court’s judgment.”
Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case, as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges could assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already said Israel has committed acts of genocide in Gaza.
A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay .
Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration . However, the administration of Donald Trump has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.
The US state department said in a statement that it would study the ICJ’s decision “to fully assess its implications” and that “the proper interpretation of the genocide convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicisation of the ICJ”.
It reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”.

Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

The Grand Theft Auto games never actually taught someone how to knock over a bank or survive a shootout with police, but the latest storyline in the franchise serves up some valuable lessons about what it means to be in a loving and committed relationship.
This isn’t sitting well with a histrionic minority of right-wing gamers who have been warning for months that GTA VI would be intolerably “woke.” While their attempt at a manufactured backlash is going even more poorly than the one that greeted Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey this summer (the day of its official release, the game is already closing in on 20 million copies sold and $2 billion in revenue ), these streamers and commentators are throwing tantrums about gender politics anyway.
“RIP GTA,” one X user somberly concluded . “Killed by women.”
In case you’re among the handful of skeptics who didn’t launch their single-player campaign in GTA VI at midnight last night after 13 years of desperate anticipation: This latest installment in the satirical crime-caper series is led by dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, a couple whose meet-cute involves them both trying to jack the same car. Living together in a fictionalized version of South Florida, they look to get by on the wrong side of the law—but the player must also negotiate their emotional bond through domestic chores and acts of affection.
“This game is such woke slop,” wrote one blue-check user on X who has posted almost nothing besides negative reactions to the game for the past week. The post included a screenshot of a fully optional GTA VI mission that describes how the Lucia character will appreciate a flower delivery and indicates with a heart icon that the action will strengthen feelings between her and Jason.
Other choices you can make as Jason to get closer to Lucia (sex is very much on the table) include picking up groceries, getting a haircut or beard trim, gifting her a piece of jewelry, and repainting walls in the house.
The concept of role-playing as a nice and non-performatively masculine boyfriend has come as a rude shock to those more interested in explosions and mayhem. The right-wing streamer Zack Hoyt, known online as Asmongold, was dumbfounded to find himself unclogging a sink in a scene where Jason is trying to collect back rent from a tenant who refuses the money until the plumbing is fixed. “I actually have to fucking fix this bitch’s sink?” Hoyt asked on stream. “Why can’t she do this?” Elsewhere, when running errands for Lucia as Jason, Hoyt referred to GTA VI as a “cuck simulator.” (That Hoyt thinks caring for a romantic partner makes someone a cuckold is perhaps an unfortunate glimpse into his dating history.)
More frustrated responses to the massively popular GTA VI came from looksmaxxing influencer Braden Peters, aka Clavicular, (the game required too much “simping for girls,” the streamer, currently facing multiple rape charges , complained on X), anti-woke gamer activist Mark Kern, aka Grummz (he called the housework “mundane crap”), and misinformation superspreader Dom Lucre, who falsely claimed that Rockstar had specifically made it impossible to open fire in a gay nightclub. (Washington Post critic Gene Park pointed out that the club in question was not LGBTQ-specific and that the mechanics of the game don’t allow you to shoot anyone in any kind of club.) These comments came alongside the predictable gripes over supposedly “overweight” female characters with insufficiently large breasts.
And Andrew Tate himself denounced the game in a Thursday email blast to his newsletter subscribers. “The establishment does not understand the male spirit,” he wrote from prison in Miami, where he and his brother Tristan Tate are fighting extradition to the UK on charges of rape, human trafficking, and assault. “No man wants to be a slave who breaks his back and gets nothing back.” Promoting a link to classes for building “AI systems,” he exhorted his readers: “Put down the game controller.”
If the Tates, incels, and other far-right reactionaries of the world are so bent out of shape, it’s probably because whereas GTA once punched down at marginalized groups like sex workers and transgender people , bigots and self-styled alpha males are now the butt of the joke. The Vice City of GTA VI is bristling with parodies of toxic manosphere content and crypto scams. Random characters on the street will spout MAGA-coded conspiracy theories and call you a “libtard” or “commie socialist” if you walk into them. These touches seem to have made the game into “a bug zapper for chuds,” as one Bluesky user put it . (That hasn’t stopped Republicans and Trump allies from trying and failing to score political points with the game.)
Yet the provocation of asking guys to consider acts of service for a virtual girlfriend could prove the most revolutionary element of GTA VI .
It’s not that games like The Sims haven’t explored this territory before, and Rockstar’s own Red Dead Redemption franchise paid similar attention to quotidian detail. In those frontier-set narratives, your cowboy character had to make coffee over campfires and even clean up manure in barns. By addressing characters’ most basic needs—you can even manage personal hygiene by showering— GTA VI recalls some of the slower and quieter aspects of that franchise.
What’s truly remarkable, though, is that adult men who grew up indulging their most selfish and sociopathic instincts in the older GTA games have had their nostalgia for those escapades cleverly complicated with real-life problems. They can still steal cars, sell drugs, and rise through the ranks of a seedy underworld. That will always be the appeal of the series, which is now asking eternally aggrieved culture warriors to consider a vital question: What if you didn’t have to do it alone?

US President Donald Trump left China on Thursday without meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, a get-together he had sought during his visit to Shenzhen for a rare three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
Trump had repeatedly raised the possibility of meeting Kim during his Asia trip, although a White House official had said no such meeting was planned.
“We may meet with Kim Jong-un also, so that'll be good,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday.
Meanwhile, Kim inspected sites in North Korea’s South Hamgyong province on Tuesday and Wednesday, according to South Korean news agency Newsis.
Although the three leaders agreed to pursue dialogue on nuclear risk reduction and non-proliferation, the joint “peace declaration” made no explicit reference to the Korean Peninsula or Taiwan.
However, Chinese state news agency Xinhua later reported that the three leaders had exchanged views on the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, nuclear non-proliferation and the situation in the Middle East.
The summit has fuelled concerns in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan that major powers could make decisions affecting regional security without consulting those directly affected.
Before the three-way meeting, South Korean media compared it to the Yalta Conference in 1945, where leaders of the US, the UK and the Soviet Union discussed the post-war international order.
Seoul has been keen to avoid major powers making decisions on the Korean peninsula without its involvement.
Although the omission of the Korean peninsula from the declaration has somewhat alleviated concerns over a second Yalta, it has raised concerns that denuclearisation is slipping down the major powers’ diplomatic agenda, according to South Korean news outlet Money Today.
Park Won-gon, a professor of North Korean studies at Ewha Womans University, told the outlet that China and Russia may have sided with Pyongyang.
Kim Jae-chun, a professor at Sogang University, said the three powers view North Korea’s nuclear programme very differently.
However, Newsis suggested that the absence of a Trump-Kim meeting for the second consecutive year may ease concerns over potential US recognition of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung reiterated, during Thursday’s APEC summit, the importance of achieving peace and stability on the Korean peninsula to bring prosperity to the region.
The three-way meeting has raised concerns in Japan, where relations with Beijing are tense.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi exchanged greetings with Xi during APEC, but the two leaders did not meet formally.
A Japanese ruling-party lawmaker said Japan’s exclusion from the three-way meeting could be seen as a diplomatic setback, Fuji TV reported.
However, Takaichi said at a press briefing in Shenzhen that she did not believe Japan’s interests would be undermined by the summit, Japanese broadcaster TBS reported.
Takaichi is also arranging a phone call with Trump to discuss the outcome of his talks with Xi and Putin and reaffirm bilateral cooperation, TV Asahi reported, citing Japanese government sources.
Japanese media also highlighted the three powers’ position on the International Criminal Court (ICC), which is currently headed by Japanese judge Tomoko Akane.
The joint declaration called for respect for the immunity of state officials and said that the ICC and similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction.
In March 2023, the court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.
As with South Korea, mentions of "Yalta 2.0" emerged in Taiwanese media in the lead-up to the meeting. Taiwanese broadcaster TVBS highlighted concerns that Taiwan could be used as a bargaining chip in the negotiations.
The question of Taiwan was raised in the bilateral meeting between Xi and Trump earlier on Thursday.
Tsai Jung-hsiang, a professor of political science at National Chung Cheng University in Taiwan, told the island’s Central News Agency that the US and China have very different views on strategic stability.
While Trump has aimed to avoid conflict over Taiwan during his time in office, Xi wanted the US to recognise Beijing’s position on sovereignty and territorial integrity, Tsai said.
However, he said he did not expect any changes to US policy regarding Taiwan as a result of the meeting.
State-run media in China said the three-way meeting allowed the three major powers to work together to promote international security and stability.
Xi said the meeting was “positive, constructive and fruitful”, as the three nations were committed to “world peace”, Xinhua reported.
Earlier, Xi said the three nations should hold regular high-level meetings and establish mechanisms to prevent and manage crises.
Neither proposal was explicitly included in the four-point peace declaration.

The International Court of Justice has upheld large parts of a genocide case against Myanmar linked to the 2017 conflict with its Rohingya minority. It called for it to pay reparations and let refugees return safely.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide .
The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state .
The judges also found the country guilty of a series of other more specific violations by majority rulings.
"On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the Court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of... the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa said that Myanmar should make efforts to pay reparations to victims or their associates where possible and appropriate.
He also called for it to facilitate the safe return of refugees, and to take measures to investigate and, if necessary, prosecute individual wrongdoing by its nationals and security forces.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The ICJ said in its consideration, the Rohingya constituted a distinct ethnic group with their own defining language and culture, as well as self-identifying as such. This means they qualified as a protected group for the purposes of international laws against genocide.
Myanmar's security forces "killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated acts of sexual violence, as well as extreme violence against children," and also attacked Rohingya as they tried to flee the fighting, the ICJ's Iwasawa said.
"The court is fully convinced that the 2017 clearance operations caused serious bodily and mental harm to a significant number of the protected group," Judge Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa also said that some civilian participation in the clearance operations could not necessarily be considered state-ordered or state-sanctioned behavior. But the court found that the government and security forces also made no meaningful efforts to prevent non-Rohingya civilian atrocities and fanned the flames of ethnic and religious tension.
At one point, reading the details of the findings, Iwasawa noted "Myanmar's failure, genuinely to investigate the alleged atrocities, and its refusal to facilitate access to evidence and witnesses, or provide information requested."
He said this meant it was possible the court did not have reliable knowledge of information available only from within Myanmar to which it was not given access.
There was no immediate response from the government in Myanmar or the military, which is regarded as the real underlying power.
Rohingya activist Yasmin Ullah — a Canadian citizen since 2016 but who was born in Rakhine state and who was a member of Gambia's delegation that filed the ICJ case — called the verdict more important for the world than for her community.
"The Rohingya never needed a court to tell us what happened to us," she said. "We needed the world to hear it, and today it has."
Wai Wai Nu, a Rohingya activist who directs the Women's Peace Network NGO, said the world's highest court's finding followed "decades" when "the Burmese military tried to erase our identity, deny our existence and dismiss our suffering."
And the co-chair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council, Nay San Lwin, said that for Rohingya people, "justice means the restoration of our citizenship, recognition of our identity and our safe and dignified return home."
Myanmar's shadow national unity government, which includes remnants of former President Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy Party, said it "respects the authority" of the ICJ.
It said that since the beginning of the "revolution against military dictatorship" in 2021, it had affirmed its "commitment to the rule of law, human rights, justice and states' obligations to prevent and punish genocide."
Myanmar was under nominally civilian rule at the time of the atrocities, but the extent to which Suu Kyi's government held sway over the military and its actions is debatable.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed Thursday's verdict, calling it a "powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and noting it was the first verdict of its kind against a state.
"Myanmar must act in accordance with its obligation to comply with the Court's decision," Guterres said in a statement, adding that this includes "the safe, voluntary and dignified return [of Rohingya] to their place of residence nad reunification of families."
Gambia's Justice Minister Dawda Jallow, who attended the hearing, spoke to reporters afterward at the Peace Palace in The Hague.
"The victory belongs to the Rohingya," Jallow said. "They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe."
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband issued a statement saying the former colonial power was "taking immediate action today in light of this judgment."
Miliband said Britain would expel Myanmar's defense attache in London and was calling for a special UN Security Council session in response. He called on Myanmar to "comply fully with the judgment," and on the international community to "play its part in supporting implementation, accountability, and justice for the Rohingya."
UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the ruling "clearly concludes the State of Myanmar stands responsible for one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind."
The case centers around the military crackdown in Rakhine state on the country's western coastline against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.
Violence had been brewing for several years beforehand, but the most intense phase of the military crackdown in the north of region was triggered by a coordinated attack by a Muslim militia group against several police and military installations and personnel in August 2017.
A UN fact finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the military clearance operations that followed. Around 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh, where most still reside in the world's largest refugee camp .
Gambia filed the complaint at The Hague in 2019, alleging a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder designed to wipe out the Rohingya minority in whole or in part.
Myanmar's influential military, now back in full de facto control of the country albeit amid a long-running civil war, has maintained that it was engaged in a legitimate counterinsurgency.
Aung San Suu Kyi , who was the civilian president at the time, took a slightly more nuanced stance, but nevertheless traveled to The Hague to contest the charges, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."
The case is likely to draw close attention from those pursuing ICJ prosecutions against Israel and Benjamin Netanyahu for the war in Gaza and against Russia and Vladimir Putin for the invasion of Ukraine.

Nadella'ya göre program, çalışanların doğrudan yapay zeka ile değiştirilmesinden ziyade Microsoft'un yapay zeka merkezli yeni çalışma düzenine geçişinin bir parçası.

Microsoft İnsan Kaynakları Başkanı Amy Coleman tarafından 26 Ekim'de paylaşılan resmi açıklamaya göre program; ABD, Kanada, Birleşik Krallık ve Hindistan 'daki belirli ekiplerde, şirket içindeki 70. seviye ve altındaki çalışanları kapsıyor. Satya Nadella, New York Times'ın DealBook Summit etkinliğinde yaptığı açıklamalarda, programın temel amaçlarından birinin çalışanların kariyerleriyle ilgili seçim yapabildiklerini hissetmelerini sağlamak olduğunu dile getirdi.Nadella, Microsoft'un çalışanları doğrudan yapay zekayla değiştirmeye çalışmadığını; bunun yerine çalışanların yapay zekayı kullandığı ve giderek daha fazla yapay zeka sistemini yönettiği bir şirket yapısına geçmeye çalıştığını belirtti.
Nadella'nın verdiği örneklerden biri yazılım mühendisliği oldu. Microsoft CEO'suna göre yapay zekanın yazılım geliştirme becerilerinin hızla ilerlemesi, yazılım mühendislerine duyulan ihtiyacı ortadan kaldırmıyor. Ancak ekiplerin nasıl organize edildiği ve mühendislerin günlük olarak yaptığı işler değişiyor. Nadella, bu dönüşümün bazı çalışanlar açısından zor olabileceğini de kabul ediyor.

Nadella, geçtiğimiz hafta The Pragmatic Engineer podcast'inde yaptığı açıklamalarda da yapay zekanın şirket içindeki ekip büyüklüklerini ve iş akışlarını değiştireceğinin sinyalini vermişti. Microsoft'un 200 binden fazla çalışanının önünde hâlâ önemli fırsatlar bulunduğunu belirten Nadella, bu fırsatların biçiminin geçmiştekinden farklı olacağını ifade etti.
Nadella'ya göre Microsoft içerisindeki bütün ekipler yapay zeka dönüşümüne aynı hızda ayak uydurmuş değil. Microsoft'un resmi açıklamasında da gönüllü ayrılık programının her ekip için geçerli olmadığı belirtiliyor. Şirket, gönüllü ayrılığın yanı sıra çalışanların yeni beceriler kazanmasına ve Microsoft içinde farklı pozisyonlara geçmesine yönelik çalışmalarını sürdüreceğini belirtiyor.

Watch: What did Trump, Xi and Putin get out of their historic meeting?
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.
The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.
In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.
Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".
Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.
In the same post, the president announced he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.
While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".
He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".
Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.
Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.
Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".
Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.
China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.
Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.
Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.
"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."
Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".
It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."
Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.
He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".
Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".
He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.
As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.
Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine.
In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.
There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.
The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two.
"Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2.
"And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."
The three presidents spoke behind closed doors at the Kylin Villa, the exclusive resort in Shenzhen
The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi.
"Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."
Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.
It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".
Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.
Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.
The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.
US lawmakers responded with frustration to Trump's warmth towards America's geopolitical adversaries.
"I was encouraged by some of the commitments that came out of the President's meetings in Asia, particularly the recognition that nuclear war must never be fought," Republican Senator John Curtis said in an emailed statement to the BBC.
But Curtis also said he was concerned about Trump's approach to the foreign leaders, adding that "Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends".
"We should not treat them as though they share our values or interests," Curtis, who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, added.
"Doing so risks undermining our national security, weakening trust with our allies, and sending the wrong message about where America stands."
Jeanne Shaheen, a ranking Democratic member on the same committee, chose harsher words in her comment.
"President Trump's 'friend' is a murderous war criminal," she wrote on X.

At least one person has died, and dozens more are missing after a boat carrying around 100 migrants capsized off the coast of Senegal while attempting to reach Spain, local officials have said.
The latest incident, which is thought to have happened in the early hours of Wednesday morning, comes amid a surge in departures towards the Canary Islands, with more than 11,000 people reaching the archipelago in the first half of November alone.
The boat, described by some sources as “rickety”, sank off the coast of Yenne, a town south of the Senegalese capital, Dakar.
“The accident happened around 3 a.m.," said Ousmane Sène, secretary general of the Yenne mayor's office.
Sène added that firefighters recovered one body while police arrested one survivor.
According to other survivors, there were around 100 people on board at the time it sank.
Sène confirmed that two other bodies were also recovered in nearby villages, but it’s not clear if they were people who drowned in this particular incident.
Recently, Senegalese coastal areas have become major departure points for migrants attempting the treacherous sea journey to Europe. Many of them are hoping to reach Spain’s Canary Islands, an archipelago off West Africa which lies more than 1,000 kilometres south of the European mainland.
According to Spanish government figures, more than 11,000 migrants reached the Canaries in the first half of November – that number was more than half the total for all of 2025.
This week’s sinking comes shortly after a disaster which saw at least 39 people die after a migrant boat sank near the town of Kébémer in northern Senegal.
Senegalese authorities are making efforts to crack down on people attempting the dangerous migration route and have made dozens of arrests.
On Wednesday, the country’s navy said it had “rescued” over 1,400 migrants at sea in just 48 hours.
Also on Wednesday, Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye spoke out against the resurgence of migrant departures toward Europe and called for strengthened controls along Senegal's coasts, too.
“The acceleration and complexity of irregular migration demonstrate the urgency for the government to intensify... the diligent and efficient implementation of public policies concerning youth, education, vocational training, youth employment and entrepreneurship, as well as the economic empowerment of women,” said Faye.

Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat said to be carrying between 50 and 100 migrants capsized in the Atlantic Ocean.
Four bodies have reportedly been recovered so far. Dozens of people are still missing.
Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.
This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.
Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).
"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.
A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.
However, a local official told Reuters news agency it was carrying 50 people, adding that the boat hit a rock as migrants were transferring from small fishing boats to a larger vessel.
Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.
At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.
He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.
Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.
Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.
The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.
It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.
The Senegalese navy said it had rescued more than 1,400 people on Monday and Tuesday this week.
As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.
They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.
Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.
They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.
On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.
It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

Four bodies have been recovered after a migrant boat capsized off Senegal’s coast, as authorities continue searching for survivors amid fears that the death toll could rise significantly.
Boubacar Seye, president of the nonprofit Horizons Sans Frontieres, confirmed the latest death toll to the Reuters news agency on Thursday, a day after the vessel capsized near the coastal town of Yenne, south of Dakar.
A local official said at least 50 people were aboard the boat, which struck a rock while migrants were being transferred from smaller fishing vessels to a larger wooden pirogue.
The incident comes amid an intensifying wave of attempted Atlantic crossings from West Africa to Spain’s Canary Islands, with migrant boats being intercepted or rescued almost daily.
New figures from Spain’s Interior Ministry show that 24,364 migrants reached the Canary Islands between January 1 and November 15, compared with 14,690 during the same period last year, an increase of nearly two-thirds.
The ministry had recorded just 13,327 arrivals by the end of October, meaning 11,037 people reached the archipelago in the first 15 days of November alone.
The surge has persisted despite extensive maritime operations. Senegal’s navy said it had rescued or intercepted 1,424 people on November 16 and 17, including passengers aboard nine fishing boats, according to the Senegalese Press Agency (APS).
Cheikh Sadibou Senghor, head of Senegal’s National Division for Combating Migrant Smuggling, said authorities had intercepted 6,889 people in operations linked to irregular migration, prevented 107 departures and dismantled 88 smuggling networks between January and November, APS reported.
Just days before the boat capsized, authorities announced the dismantling of a suspected migrant-smuggling network in Yenne itself, arresting 14 people and seizing two boats, three engines and 12.5 million CFA francs ($22,000), according to APS.
The United Nations refugee agency said nearly 600 people had died trying to reach the Canary Islands from West Africa so far this year, highlighting the dangers of the increasingly busy migration route.
As authorities struggle to contain the surge, Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has called for greater efforts to improve employment opportunities for young people.
At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Faye requested a detailed assessment of the challenges facing efforts to curb irregular migration, according to a government statement cited by Reuters.
But Seye warned that tougher enforcement measures alone would not prevent further tragedies.
“We need to wake up to the gravity of the situation. The strategy deployed until now is not working,” he told Reuters.

Zoo staff tried a colonoscopy, vibration plate and other procedures to aid the hippo in passing the hat to no avail
Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has died after efforts to remove a knitted hat that she swallowed after it fell into her enclosure proved unsuccessful.
“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo wrote in a post on social media .
With surgery too risky for full-grown hippos such as Fiona, who weighed in the region of 2,500lb (1,113kg), veterinarians tried an alternative method of getting the hat to pass through her system.
The hat fell near Fiona when a visitor to the Cincinnati zoo tossed it in the air, after which it bounced off a ceiling fan and fell into the enclosure, according to the Associated Press . Fiona ate the hat and was initially asymptomatic.
Days later, however, she began to lose appetite and staff at the zoo were forced to feed Fiona more in the hope that she would eventually get the hat through her digestive system.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover,” the zoo statement said.
The zoo announced on Wednesday that the animal care team was using a vibration plate from a horse farm to help move things along, according to the Associated Press .
Fiona was sedated a second time on Tuesday for evaluation. After an ultrasound, veterinarians could see her intestines still trying to push the hat through. They also used a 9ft scope colonoscopy to view her intestines.
“The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the zoo had said on social media . Fiona remained out of her enclosure while she was receiving treatment.
Footage from the procedure released by the zoo on Wednesday shows her snorting and moving around her enclosure, which vets said was a sign of progress. Her hydration levels were being monitored.
“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked, and they were happy to see her respond. Thank you for your continued love and concern for Fiona and her dedicated care team,” the zoo said .
This wasn’t the first time Fiona’s health had been at risk. She became a global sensation after her premature birth in 2017, when she couldn’t stand on her own.
Hopes for Fiona’s recovery had garnered support from across the country including, apparently, from Timothy, another hippo at the San Antonio zoo. Timothy had sent well wishes via Instagram. “I know you’ve got some amazing people looking after you. We’re sending lots of love from Texas to the most beautiful hippo in the world. Hope you’re feeling more like yourself soon!”
Zoo staff published a message on social media reminding visitors to be careful when near habitats and to secure belongings.
Fiona was born six weeks premature at just 29lb (13.2kgs), falling below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time. Because she was initially too weak to nurse, Cincinnati Zoo staff hand-milked her mother while documenting Fiona’s recovery through photos and videos that captivated the internet.
Her survival then offered a much-needed positive chapter for the zoo following months of intense public backlash over the fatal shooting of Harambe , the silverback gorilla killed after a child breached his enclosure.
Wildlife facilities have long warned of the dangers posed by foreign objects dropped or blown into animal habitats. Past incidents have demonstrated the fatal risks involved, including a rare antelope that choked to death on a plastic cap of a snack pouch at a Tennessee zoo two years ago, and a polar bear at a German zoo that died in 2014 after swallowing a visitor’s dropped jacket.

From premature baby to social media star - Famed Cincinnati Zoo hippo Fiona dies
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona has died just days after swallowing a knitted hat that slipped into her enclosure.
"It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said on Thursday afternoon.
Fiona, who became a social media star after her premature birth in 2017, swallowed the hat about 10 days ago and required emergency care.
The vet staff "tried everything they could to help her" but "it was ultimately too much to overcome", the zoo said.
Fiona initially seemed fine after swallowing the hat more than a week ago
"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."
Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.
"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.
While she seemed fine at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.
An ultrasound before her death showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine. A zookeeper said surgery was not an option for full-grown hippos and "our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own".
The zoo also tried a different approach to attempt to get the hat to pass by encouraging Fiona to stand on a vibration plate platform borrowed from a local horse farm.
"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said.
Fiona was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
Her death is also very premature, with hippos normally living up to 50 years in human care, according to the zoo.
"Although this was not an intentional incident, of which, regrettably, there are many, Fiona's painful death is a tragic reminder that everyone should behave carefully and respectfully around animals," Debbie Metzler, the Managing Director of Captive Wildlife for the animal rights group Peta.
"Peta expects that the zoo will review its protocols to help prevent anything like this from happening again, and we urge every visitor to secure their belongings and never toss objects near an animal's enclosure."
As well as being famous online, Fiona's story inspired an ice cream flavour and a character in Cincinnati's ballet.
Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval said Fiona "was a symbol of perseverance and joy" in the city.
"She brought smiles to so many faces, from kids to parents to visitors from around the world," he wrote on X. "Our city is heartbroken, but we couldn't be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole."
